Every black hole we have studied so far announced itself with light — a quasar
outshining its galaxy, a star swinging around something invisible, gas heated
until it glowed. Light is not the only signal a black hole can send. When two
of them orbit each other and finally merge, they radiate energy directly into
the geometry of spacetime, and for a fraction of a second a single pair of
black holes can outshine every star in the observable universe in a form of
radiation that passes straight through the Earth. **This lecture works out what
a gravitational wave is, how large an effect it produces when it arrives, how
we measure something that small, and why the frequency you listen at decides
which black holes you can hear.**

## Ripples in spacetime

An accelerating electric charge radiates electromagnetic waves. General
relativity says that an accelerating *mass* should do something analogous: a
gravitational field that changes rapidly enough produces ripples in the
curvature of spacetime, and those ripples travel outward at the speed of light.
They are **gravitational waves**.

The analogy is close, and worth drawing carefully, because the one place it
breaks down is the important place. An electromagnetic wave is an oscillation
of the electric and magnetic fields, and those fields live *in* spacetime.
A gravitational wave is an oscillation *of* spacetime. There is no medium
underneath it. What is waving is the thing that distances are measured with.

### Why the lowest note is the quadrupole

Electromagnetic radiation is usually produced by a **dipole**: separate a
positive and a negative charge, shake them back and forth, and the changing
dipole moment radiates. Gravity cannot do that, and the reason is a
conservation law.

Gravity has no negative mass, so the gravitational analogue of the total charge
is the **total mass**, and the total mass of an isolated system does not
change. A quantity that does not change cannot oscillate, so there is no
monopole radiation. Go one step up and the gravitational analogue of the dipole
moment turns out to be the total **momentum** of the system, and that does not
change either. So there is no dipole radiation.

The first moment that is free to vary is the next one, the **quadrupole**,
which measures how the mass is *distributed* — roughly, how far the system
departs from a sphere, and along which axis. So:

> A system radiates gravitational waves only if its mass quadrupole moment
> changes with time.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about what a perfectly spherical star does when it collapses"}
It radiates no gravitational waves at all.

A sphere that shrinks is still a sphere. Its mass is unchanged, its momentum is
unchanged, and its quadrupole moment — which is a statement about departures
from sphericity — is unchanged too. Every moment that could radiate is
constant, so nothing is emitted, no matter how violent the collapse is or how
much matter is involved.

This is a real astrophysical constraint rather than a technicality. A
supernova radiates gravitational waves only to the extent that its collapse is
*lopsided*, which is why predicting the signal from one is so much harder than
predicting the signal from a binary. A binary, by contrast, is about as far
from spherical as a system can be, and it advertises the fact twice per orbit.
:::

### Two polarizations

Because the source is a quadrupole, the wave it makes does something a light
wave does not. A gravitational wave traveling toward you stretches space along
one direction across your line of sight and squeezes it along the
perpendicular direction, then reverses: squeeze where it stretched, stretch
where it squeezed.

Drop a ring of free particles in the path of one and watch. The ring flattens
into an ellipse, returns to a circle, then flattens into an ellipse at right
angles to the first. Nothing pushes the particles; the distances between them
simply change, because the geometry between them is changing.

There are two independent ways of doing this, called the two **polarizations**.
The **plus** polarization, written $h_+$, stretches and squeezes along the
horizontal and vertical axes. The **cross** polarization, $h_\times$, does the
same thing along axes rotated by 45°. Any gravitational wave is a combination
of the two, and the amounts of each depend on the orientation of the source.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
[Note the 45°. The two polarizations of a light wave are at 90° to each other,
because a light wave is built from a vector. A gravitational wave is built from
a quadrupole, whose pattern repeats twice per full turn, so its two independent
states are half as far apart.]{.aside}
:::

The numbers $h_+$ and $h_\times$ are the amplitude of the wave. They are
*fractional* changes in length — the fraction by which the ring is stretched —
so they are pure numbers, and as we are about to see they are extraordinarily
small ones.

### How the two kinds of radiation compare

Nearly every instinct built up from doing astronomy with light has to be
retuned for gravitational waves, and the table below is worth reading slowly.
The differences are not incidental; each one changes what an observation can
and cannot tell you.

| | Electromagnetic waves | Gravitational waves |
|---|---|---|
| What is waving | fields, with spacetime as the medium | spacetime itself |
| What produces them | incoherent superposition of many atoms and molecules | coherent motion of enormous masses |
| Wavelength vs source | small compared with the source, so we get images | comparable to the source, so the sky position is poorly resolved |
| Interaction with matter | absorbed, scattered and dispersed | almost none, and nothing shields them |
| Frequencies | $10^{6}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and up | $10^{4}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and down |
| What a detector measures | intensity, or amplitude at radio frequencies | amplitude, always |
| Field of view | usually a small solid angle | very nearly the whole sky at once |

Two of those rows deserve emphasis. **Nothing shields a gravitational wave.**
Dust that hides the center of our Galaxy at visible wavelengths is completely
transparent to them, and so is the matter of a collapsing stellar core, and so
is the Earth — the wave that LIGO detected passed through the whole planet on
its way from Louisiana to Washington without measurable loss. And **a
gravitational-wave detector sees almost the entire sky at once**, which makes
it less like a telescope than like a microphone. You do not point it. You turn
it on and wait.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-ripples}

1. Explain in two or three sentences why a single star spinning about its axis,
   perfectly axisymmetric, emits no gravitational waves — while the same star
   with a mountain on one side does.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   An axisymmetric star spinning about its symmetry axis presents exactly the
   same mass distribution at every instant, so its quadrupole moment is
   constant in time and nothing is radiated. A mountain breaks the symmetry:
   as the star turns, the departure from axisymmetry sweeps around with it, so
   the quadrupole moment measured by a distant observer oscillates at the spin
   frequency and the star radiates. This is a real search target — a pulsar
   with a mountain a few centimeters high would be detectable.
   :::

2. The Earth orbiting the Sun is a binary system with a time-varying mass
   quadrupole, so it must radiate gravitational waves. Without calculating
   anything, list the three properties of the Earth–Sun system from the table
   in this section that make the strain at a distant detector far too small to
   measure, and say in each case whether that property is large or small.

3. A gravitational wave arrives traveling straight down through your body, with
   the plus polarization aligned so that it stretches you left-to-right.

   a. What is happening to your height at that instant?
   b. Half a period later, what is happening to your height?
   c. Does the wave change your front-to-back thickness?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** Your height is being squeezed, because the wave stretches along one
   transverse direction and squeezes along the perpendicular transverse one.
   **(b)** The two have swapped: your height is being stretched and your width
   squeezed. **(c)** No. Front-to-back is along the direction the wave is
   traveling, and gravitational waves are transverse — the distortion is
   entirely across the line of propagation.
   :::

:::

## The first evidence was indirect

Gravitational waves were predicted in 1916 and not detected directly until
2015. For most of that century the best evidence that they exist at all came
from watching an orbit shrink.

### Pulsars are excellent clocks

A **pulsar** is a rapidly rotating neutron star with a strong magnetic field.
Radiation streams out along the magnetic axis in two narrow beams, and because
the magnetic axis is tilted away from the rotation axis, those beams sweep
around the sky like a lighthouse. If one of them happens to cross the Earth, we
see a pulse once per rotation.

What makes a pulsar valuable is not the pulses but their regularity. A neutron
star is a solar mass of material in a sphere about ten kilometers across, so
its moment of inertia is enormous and there is almost nothing that can
perturb its spin. Some pulsars keep time well enough to rival an atomic clock.

### The Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar

In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found a pulsar whose pulse arrival
times were not steady: they drifted early and late on a cycle of about eight
hours [@hulse1975]. The explanation is that the pulsar is in orbit with another
neutron star, and the drift is the changing light-travel time across the orbit.
It was the first binary pulsar known, and it won them the 1993 Nobel Prize in
Physics.

The system's numbers are what make it useful:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Spin period | $59\ \mathrm{ms}$ — about 17 rotations per second |
| Orbital period | $7.75\ \mathrm{hours}$ |
| Orbital separation | roughly the radius of the Sun |
| Orbital speed | of order $10^{-3}\,c$ |

Two neutron stars, moving fast, close together, in a decidedly non-spherical
configuration: a textbook time-varying quadrupole. General relativity therefore
demands that the system radiate gravitational waves, lose orbital energy, and
spiral inward — and a smaller orbit means a shorter period.

Measuring a change in an eight-hour period directly would be hopeless. But the
effect **accumulates**. If each orbit is a fraction of a millisecond short, the
shortfall adds up orbit after orbit, and after a few years the pulsar arrives at
closest approach measurably earlier than a constant period would predict.
Plotting that accumulated shift against time gives a curve that bends away from
the horizontal, and the shape of the bend is a prediction of general relativity
with no adjustable parameters.

The measurement has now been running for fifty years. Over the first thirty of
them the accumulated shift reached about **40 seconds**, and it tracked the
general-relativistic prediction the whole way.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about what happens to the orbital speed as the orbit loses energy"}
The stars speed up.

This feels wrong the first time. The system is losing energy, and things that
lose energy usually slow down. But the total energy of a circular orbit, which
you have already met,

$$
E = -\frac{G m_1 m_2}{2 a} ,
$$

is *negative*, and it becomes more negative as the separation $a$ shrinks. So
radiating energy away makes $a$ smaller — and by Kepler's third law a smaller
orbit is a faster one.

Gravitationally bound systems behave like this generally: take energy out and
they get hotter, faster and more tightly bound. It is the same reason the
inspiral **accelerates** rather than settling down. As the orbit shrinks the
stars move faster, which makes them radiate more strongly, which shrinks the
orbit faster still. The process runs away, and the last few orbits before a
merger take milliseconds.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-indirect}

1. The Hulse–Taylor pulsar spins once every $59\ \mathrm{ms}$ and orbits its
   companion once every $7.75\ \mathrm{hours}$. How many times does it spin per
   orbit?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About $4.7 \times 10^{5}$ times. Converting the orbital period first, with
   the fractions arranged so the hours and minutes cancel,

   $$
   7.75\ \mathrm{hr} \times \frac{3600\ \mathrm{s}}{1\ \mathrm{hr}}
     = 2.79 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{s},
   $$

   and $2.79 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{s} / 0.059\ \mathrm{s} = 4.7 \times 10^{5}$,
   a pure number as a ratio of two times must be. Every one of those half a
   million pulses per orbit is a measurement, which is why the orbit is known
   so precisely.
   :::

2. Explain, in three or four sentences, why a plot of the accumulated shift in
   periastron time against year curves downward instead of following a straight
   line. Your answer should distinguish between an orbit whose period is
   constant but slightly mismeasured, and an orbit whose period is changing.

3. Suppose a binary loses energy to gravitational waves at a constant rate.
   Using $E = -Gm_1m_2/2a$, does the separation shrink at a constant rate, or
   faster and faster, or more and more slowly? Explain your reasoning.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
   Rearrange for $a$ in terms of $E$, and ask what happens to $a$ when $E$
   changes by a fixed amount, first when $a$ is large and then when $a$ is
   small.
   :::

:::

## How big is the effect

Everything so far has been qualitative. To know whether a gravitational wave
can be detected we need a number, and the quantity to put a number on is the
**strain**.

You met it in [lecture 5](../strong-gravity/index.qmd#gravitational-waves): the
strain is the fractional change in the distance between two points,

$$
h = \frac{\Delta L}{L} .
$$ {#eq-strain-10}

Two freely floating masses a distance $L$ apart will be found a distance
$L + \Delta L$ apart when the wave arrives. Strain is a pure number, it is what
a detector actually measures, and everything in this lecture eventually reduces
to estimating it.

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

Three things should make the strain bigger, and all three are visible in the
picture of two masses whirling around each other.

**Bigger masses.** The quadrupole moment measures mass times the square of a
size, so more mass means a larger quadrupole to begin with.

**Higher velocities.** What radiates is not the quadrupole moment but its rate
of *change*, twice over. A binary going around faster wrenches its mass
distribution around faster, and the emission is extremely sensitive to this.

**Nearby sources.** The amplitude falls off as one over the distance, not one
over the distance squared. That is worth pausing on, because it is the opposite
of the instinct built up from brightness. A detector measures the wave's
*amplitude*, and amplitude goes as $1/r$; it is the *energy* that goes as
$1/r^2$. The practical consequence is enormous: making a detector twice as
sensitive lets it see twice as far, which is eight times the volume and so
roughly eight times the event rate.

Put those together and the ideal source is obvious: two very massive, very
compact objects, orbiting very close to each other, as near to us as possible.
Two compact objects — black holes or neutron stars — can get close together
without touching, which ordinary stars cannot, and that is what lets them reach
speeds approaching the speed of light while still in orbit. As they orbit they
lose energy and angular momentum to gravitational waves, the orbit shrinks, the
frequency climbs, and eventually they merge.

### Mathematical explanation

The quadrupole moment of a binary of two masses $M$ separated by a distance $R$
is roughly

$$
Q \sim M R^2 ,
$$

and general relativity says that the strain a distant observer measures is set
by the *second* time derivative of that, weakened by a factor $G/c^4$ and
diluted by the distance $r$ to the source:

$$
h \sim \frac{G}{c^4 r}\, \ddot{Q} .
$$

The mass and the separation are fixed, so the time dependence is entirely in
the orbital phase, and each time derivative brings down a factor of the angular
frequency $\omega = 2\pi f_{\mathrm{orb}}$. Two derivatives give $\omega^2 =
4\pi^2 f_{\mathrm{orb}}^2$, so

$$
h \approx \frac{4\pi^2 G M R^2 f_{\mathrm{orb}}^2}{c^4 r} .
$$ {#eq-strain-binary}

That is the expression on your constants sheet, and it is an order-of-magnitude
estimate rather than an exact result — the true answer carries factors that
depend on the orientation of the orbit and on where in the sky the source is.
It gets the size right, which is what we need.

**Look at $G/c^4$.** Numerically it is about
$8 \times 10^{-50}\ \mathrm{s^2\,g^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$. There is no way to make a
laboratory source with enough mass moving fast enough to overcome a number that
small, which is why every gravitational-wave source is astrophysical.

#### Rewriting it with Kepler's third law

Equation @eq-strain-binary has three variables describing the binary — $M$, $R$
and $f_{\mathrm{orb}}$ — but they are not independent. Kepler's third law ties
them together: for two masses $M$ in a circular orbit of separation $R$,

$$
R^3 = \frac{G (2M)}{4\pi^2 f_{\mathrm{orb}}^2} ,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
R^2 = \left[ \frac{G (2M)}{4\pi^2 f_{\mathrm{orb}}^2} \right]^{2/3} .
$$

Substituting that into @eq-strain-binary and collecting the powers of
$f_{\mathrm{orb}}$ — one factor of $f^{2}$ from the derivatives and a factor
$f^{-4/3}$ from $R^2$ — gives

$$
h \propto \frac{G^{5/3} M^{5/3} f_{\mathrm{orb}}^{2/3}}{c^4 r} .
$$ {#eq-strain-scaling}

So, in words,

$$
\text{amplitude} \ \propto\
  \frac{\mathrm{mass}^{5/3} \times \mathrm{frequency}^{2/3}}{\mathrm{distance}} .
$$

The mass dependence is far stronger than the frequency dependence, which is why
the heaviest binaries dominate every band they can be seen in. The combination
of the two masses that appears here when they are not equal is called the
**chirp mass**, and it is the single best-measured property of a
gravitational-wave source: the rate at which the frequency sweeps upward
depends on it almost alone.

That last fact has a remarkable consequence. The chirp gives you the mass; the
mass and the frequency together give you the intrinsic amplitude through
@eq-strain-scaling; comparing that with the amplitude you actually measure
gives you the distance. A gravitational-wave source tells you how far away it
is without any calibration against another object — no standard candle, no
distance ladder. They are called **standard sirens**.

### Numerical exploration

Equation @eq-strain-binary applied to four binaries, spanning stellar-mass
mergers through supermassive black holes. The separation for each is fixed by
Kepler's third law from the mass and the orbital frequency, so each row is a
self-consistent system.

```{python}
#| label: strain-ladder

import math

G = 6.6732e-8          # cm^3 g^-1 s^-2
c = 2.99792456e10      # cm s^-1
M_sun = 1.9891e33      # g
pc = 3.0856e18         # cm

# name, mass of EACH object (M_sun), orbital frequency (Hz), distance (Mpc)
systems = [
    ("neutron stars, 40 Mpc",   1.4,   590.0,       40.0),
    ("GW150914",               32.5,   125.0,      410.0),
    ("100 M_sun pair",         50.0,   100.0,      400.0),
    ("supermassive pair",      5.0e8,    1.0e-9,   400.0),
]

fmt = "{:<24}{:>12}{:>12}{:>11}"
print(fmt.format("system", "separation", "f_orb (Hz)", "strain"))
for name, m, f, d in systems:
    M, r = m * M_sun, d * 1e6 * pc
    R = (G * 2 * M / (4 * math.pi**2 * f**2)) ** (1 / 3)      # Kepler
    h = 4 * math.pi**2 * G * M * R**2 * f**2 / (c**4 * r)
    sep = f"{R/1e5:.0f} km" if R < 1e17 else f"{R/pc:.3f} pc"
    print(fmt.format(name, sep, f"{f:.3g}", f"{h:.2e}"))
```

The last row is the one to stare at. A pair of supermassive black holes
produces a strain **ten thousand times larger** than the event LIGO detected,
and LIGO cannot see it at all. Why not is the subject of the next section but
one.

### Turn the knobs

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: the strain from GW150914"}
**The question.** Two black holes of about $32.5\,M_\odot$ each orbit one
another 125 times per second at a distance of $410\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ from Earth.
What strain do they produce here?

The givens are the mass of each object, $M = 32.5\,M_\odot$, the orbital
frequency $f_{\mathrm{orb}} = 125\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and the distance
$r = 410\ \mathrm{Mpc}$. Equation @eq-strain-binary also needs the separation
$R$, which is not given — so it has to come from Kepler's third law first.

**The separation.** For two masses $M$ in a circular orbit,

$$
R^3 = \frac{G\,(2M)}{4\pi^2 f_{\mathrm{orb}}^2} .
$$

Substitute with the units attached, and no arithmetic yet. The total mass is

$$
2M = 65 \times 1.989 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}
   = 1.29 \times 10^{35}\ \mathrm{g},
$$

so

$$
R^3 = \frac{\left(6.673 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
            \left(1.29 \times 10^{35}\ \mathrm{g}\right)}
           {4\pi^2 \left(125\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\right)^2} .
$$

Cancel the units before touching the numbers. The grams cancel between $G$ and
the mass, leaving $\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}$ on top; the bottom is
$\mathrm{s^{-2}}$; so the inverse seconds squared cancel as well and we are
left with $\mathrm{cm^3}$. *Do the units make sense?* We want a separation,
which is a length, and the cube root of a volume is a length, so yes.

$$
R^3 = \frac{8.63 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}}
           {1.54 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}}
    = 5.59 \times 10^{21}\ \mathrm{cm^3} ,
$$

$$
R = 1.77 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{cm} = 177\ \mathrm{km} .
$$

Two black holes of thirty-odd solar masses, 177 kilometers apart. For
comparison, the Schwarzschild radius of a $65\,M_\odot$ black hole is about
190 kilometers — so at this moment the two holes are nearly touching, and the
merger is milliseconds away.

**The strain.** Now @eq-strain-binary. The distance in centimeters, with the
conversion fractions arranged so that the megaparsecs and parsecs cancel, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
r &= 410\ \mathrm{Mpc}
     \times \frac{10^{6}\ \mathrm{pc}}{1\ \mathrm{Mpc}}
     \times \frac{3.086 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{pc}} \\[0.8em]
  &= 1.27 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{cm} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting, with the units still attached:

$$
h \approx \frac{4\pi^2
  \left(6.673\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
  \left(6.46\times10^{34}\ \mathrm{g}\right)
  \left(1.77\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^2
  \left(125\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\right)^2}
  {\left(3.00\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^4
  \left(1.27\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)} .
$$

Cancel the units. On top: $\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times \mathrm{g}
\times \mathrm{cm^2} \times \mathrm{s^{-2}} = \mathrm{cm^5\,s^{-4}}$. On the
bottom: $\mathrm{cm^4\,s^{-4}} \times \mathrm{cm} = \mathrm{cm^5\,s^{-4}}$.
Everything cancels. *Do the units make sense?* Strain is a fractional change in
length, which is a pure number, so yes — and if anything had survived we would
know we had gone wrong before multiplying a single digit.

$$
h \approx \frac{6.74 \times 10^{46}}{1.03 \times 10^{69}}
  = 6.6 \times 10^{-23} \cdot 10^{1.4}
  \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-21} .
$$

The measured peak strain of GW150914 was about $10^{-21}$. An
order-of-magnitude formula, three numbers read off a press release, and we land
within a factor of two of the real measurement.
::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-strain}

1. Two neutron stars, each of mass $1.4\,M_\odot$, are in a circular orbit
   $30\ \mathrm{km}$ apart. The system is $40\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ away.

   a. Use Kepler's third law to find the orbital frequency, in Hz.
   b. Use @eq-strain-binary to find the strain at Earth.
   c. LIGO's arms are $4\ \mathrm{km}$ long. By how much does this wave change
      the length of one arm? Compare it with the size of a proton, about
      $10^{-13}\ \mathrm{cm}$.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   **(a)** Kepler's third law in the form on the constants sheet uses
   astronomical units, years and solar masses, so convert the separation first,
   with the fraction arranged so that the centimeters cancel:

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   R &= 30\ \mathrm{km}
        \times \frac{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}
        \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{AU}}{1.496 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm}} \\[0.8em]
     &= 2.005 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{AU} .
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   The total mass is $2 \times 1.4 = 2.8\,M_\odot$. Then

   $$
   \left(\frac{P}{1\ \mathrm{yr}}\right)^2
     = \frac{(R/1\ \mathrm{AU})^3}{(M_{\mathrm{tot}}/M_\odot)}
     = \frac{8.065 \times 10^{-21}}{2.8}
     = 2.880 \times 10^{-21} ,
   $$

   a pure number on both sides, as it must be. Taking the square root,

   $$
   P = 5.367 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{yr}
       \times \frac{3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}}{1\ \mathrm{yr}}
     = 1.694 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s} ,
   $$

   so

   $$
   f_{\mathrm{orb}} = \frac{1}{P} = \boxed{590\ \mathrm{Hz}} .
   $$

   Two objects heavier than the Sun, going around each other 590 times a
   second.

   **(b)** Now @eq-strain-binary, with $M = 1.4\,M_\odot$ — the mass of *one*
   of the two, which is what appears in that formula — and the distance
   converted the same way as in the worked example,
   $r = 40\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 1.234 \times 10^{26}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Substituting
   with the units attached:

   $$
   h \approx \frac{4\pi^2
     \left(6.673\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
     \left(2.785\times10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}\right)
     \left(3.0\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^2
     \left(590\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\right)^2}
     {\left(3.00\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^4
     \left(1.234\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)} .
   $$

   The units cancel exactly as they did in the worked example, leaving a pure
   number — which is what a strain has to be. Then

   $$
   h \approx \frac{2.30 \times 10^{46}}{9.97 \times 10^{67}}
     = \boxed{2.3 \times 10^{-22}} .
   $$

   **(c)** From @eq-strain-10, $\Delta L = h L$. The strain is a pure number,
   so $\Delta L$ inherits the units of $L$ — a length, which is what a change
   in arm length had better be. Converting the arm length,

   $$
   L = 4\ \mathrm{km} \times \frac{10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{km}}
     = 4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm} ,
   $$

   $$
   \Delta L = \left(2.3 \times 10^{-22}\right)
              \left(4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)
            = \boxed{9.2 \times 10^{-17}\ \mathrm{cm}} .
   $$

   As a fraction of a proton,

   $$
   \frac{\Delta L}{r_p}
     = \frac{9.2 \times 10^{-17}\ \mathrm{cm}}{10^{-13}\ \mathrm{cm}}
     = 9.2 \times 10^{-4} ,
   $$

   a pure number, as a ratio of two lengths must be. **About a thousandth of
   the width of a proton** — which is exactly the sensitivity LIGO is built to
   reach, and this system is not hypothetical. It is GW170817.
   :::

2. Two black holes orbit each other at some separation and frequency, producing
   a strain $h$ at Earth. A second, identical pair orbits at the same
   separation and frequency but each hole is twice as massive.

   a. By what factor does the strain change, according to
      @eq-strain-binary?
   b. Such a pair cannot actually orbit at the same separation *and* the same
      frequency. Which of the two would have to change, and why?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   For (a), only one factor in @eq-strain-binary contains the mass. For (b),
   ask what Kepler's third law says about a heavier system at a fixed
   separation.

   The answers are a factor of 2, and the frequency — a heavier pair at the
   same separation must orbit faster, by $\sqrt{2}$.
   :::

3. Improved mirrors make a detector twice as sensitive, so that it can now
   register a strain half as large as before.

   a. How much further away can it detect an identical source?
   b. By what factor does the volume of space it surveys increase?
   c. Assuming sources are spread uniformly through space, by what factor does
      the detection rate increase?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** Twice as far, since $h \propto 1/r$. **(b)** Eight times, since
   volume goes as $r^3$. **(c)** Eight times. This is why a modest improvement
   in detector sensitivity produces such a dramatic jump in the number of
   events: the first LIGO observing run found three mergers, and recent runs
   find them at better than one a week.
   :::

4. Using @eq-strain-scaling, compare two binaries at the same distance and the
   same orbital frequency, one with ten times the mass of the other. Which
   produces the larger strain, and by what factor?

:::

## Catching a wave

A strain of $10^{-21}$ over four kilometers is a displacement of about
$4 \times 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Building an instrument that can measure that
is the whole problem, and the solution is to stop trying to measure a length
and measure a *difference* of two lengths instead.

### Why the detector is an L

Here is the difficulty with measuring a length directly: the ruler stretches
too. If the wave stretches the arm by one part in $10^{21}$, and you compare
the arm against a meter stick lying beside it, the meter stick is stretched by
the same fraction and the comparison shows nothing.

What saves the experiment is the fact from the first section — that a
gravitational wave stretches one transverse direction while it **squeezes** the
perpendicular one. So build two arms at right angles. When the wave arrives one
arm gets longer while the other gets shorter, and the *difference* between them
is what changes. That difference is a real, measurable quantity, and it is
twice the change in either arm alone.

That is why every ground-based gravitational-wave detector is an L.

The comparison is done with light. A laser beam is split at the corner and sent
down both arms, reflected back and forth between mirrors about 280 times so
that each beam travels an effective path of roughly 1120 kilometers, then
recombined. The arms are tuned so that the two beams cancel exactly when
nothing is happening, and the detector sits in darkness. A passing wave changes
the two path lengths by different amounts, the cancellation stops being
perfect, and light appears at the output.

![LIGO Hanford, in eastern Washington: one of the two American detectors. The
two arms run away from the corner station at right angles, each four kilometers
long, and the beam tubes are held under vacuum along their whole length. The
second American installation is at Livingston, Louisiana, three thousand
kilometers away. Photograph by the LIGO Laboratory; public
domain.](../strong-gravity/ligo-hanford-aerial.jpg){#fig-ligo-10
width="100%"
fig-alt="Aerial photograph of a low white building complex in flat, dry
scrubland. Two long straight enclosed tubes leave the building at right angles
to each other and run to the horizon, one toward the upper left and one toward
the upper right, each ending at a small outbuilding."}

### Why there has to be more than one

A single detector cannot distinguish a gravitational wave from a truck going
past, a distant earthquake, or a mirror settling. The defense is to build the
same instrument twice, three thousand kilometers apart, and require that a
signal appear at both sites within the light-travel time between them — about
ten milliseconds — with consistent amplitude and shape. Local disturbances fail
that test immediately.

More than two detectors buys something else: a **position on the sky**. The
table in the first section noted that gravitational-wave detectors have almost
no directional sensitivity, so the only handle on direction is the difference
in arrival time between widely separated sites, which fixes the source onto a
ring on the sky. Add a third site and the rings intersect. The global network
is now LIGO Hanford and Livingston, Virgo in Italy, KAGRA in Japan, GEO600 in
Germany, and LIGO-India under construction — and the reason for building
detectors on four continents is almost entirely this.

### GW150914

On **14 September 2015**, both LIGO detectors recorded a signal — first at
Livingston, and then, seven milliseconds later, at Hanford
[@abbott2016]. It lasted about 200 milliseconds in the detectors' sensitive
band.

Matching the waveform against solutions of Einstein's equations identified it
as the merger of two black holes of about $36\,M_\odot$ and $29\,M_\odot$,
leaving a single black hole of about $62\,M_\odot$. Add those up: $36 + 29 =
65$, and the remnant is 62. **About three solar masses were converted into
energy** and radiated away as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second.

![The GW150914 detection. The top row is the strain measured at each site, with
Hanford's trace overlaid on Livingston's at the right to show how well they
agree. The second row compares the measurement against a waveform computed from
general relativity for two merging black holes — the theory curve was not
fitted to the data by adjusting the physics, it was *predicted* from it. The
third row is what is left over after subtracting the model, which is noise and
nothing more. The bottom row shows frequency against time: the signal sweeps
upward as the two holes spiral closer and faster, which is the chirp. Figure by
[Rothwild](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LIGO_measurement_of_gravitational_waves_multilang.svg),
used under [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/) and
modified to show only the English
labels.](../strong-gravity/gw150914-strain.png){#fig-gw150914-10
width="100%"
fig-alt="An eight-panel scientific figure in two columns headed Hanford,
Washington and Livingston, Louisiana. The top three rows are line plots of
strain against time: a jagged trace, then a smoother trace with a shaded
uncertainty band around a matching model curve, then a flat noisy residual. The
bottom row shows two dark spectrograms in which a bright yellow-green streak
curves upward toward higher frequency at the right-hand end."}

Look at the bottom row of @fig-gw150914-10, the **chirp**. The frequency climbs
as the two black holes spiral inward, exactly as the Resolution callout in the
Hulse–Taylor section said it must: energy leaves, the orbit shrinks, the
orbital speed rises, and the emission gets stronger, which takes more energy
out still. The last few orbits of a fifty-year-long inspiral take a fifth of a
second.

And because the rate of that sweep is fixed by the chirp mass, the shape of the
curve in that panel is the mass measurement. The amplitude then gives the
distance, through @eq-strain-scaling. The entire physical description of the
event — two masses, a distance, a final mass and spin — is read off a signal
that lasted a fifth of a second and moved the mirrors by a thousandth of a
proton.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
[Two years later, in August 2017, the network caught a *neutron-star* merger,
GW170817, at about 40 Mpc [@abbott2017]. Because neutron stars are made of
matter rather than pure geometry, this one also produced light: a gamma-ray
burst two seconds later, and then an explosion that was followed by telescopes
on every continent for weeks. It is the system you estimated the strain of in
the first exercise of the previous section.]{.aside}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-ligo}

1. A gravitational wave arrives at Livingston, Louisiana and seven milliseconds
   later at Hanford, Washington, which are $3000\ \mathrm{km}$ apart.

   a. How long would light take to travel between the two sites?
   b. What does your answer, compared with the measured 7 ms, tell you about
      the direction the wave came from?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   The two sites are separated by $3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm}$, and the wave
   travels at $c$.

   The answer to (a) is $10\ \mathrm{ms}$. For (b): since 7 ms is less than 10
   ms, the wave did not travel along the line joining the two detectors. The
   ratio $7/10$ fixes the cosine of the angle between the wave's direction and
   that line, which places the source on a ring about $45°$ from the axis
   through the two sites.
   :::

2. Explain, in three or four sentences, why comparing a detector arm against a
   ruler lying beside it would not work, while comparing two perpendicular arms
   against each other does.

3. Suppose someone proposes to detect gravitational waves by building a single
   detector twice as long instead of two detectors at different sites. Give one
   thing this would improve and one thing it would not fix.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   It would improve the raw signal: $\Delta L = hL$, so doubling $L$ doubles
   the displacement to be measured for the same strain. It would not fix the
   problem the second *site* exists to solve — telling a real signal from a
   local disturbance, and getting any directional information at all. A longer
   single detector is a better instrument and still cannot claim a detection on
   its own.
   :::

:::

## The gravitational-wave spectrum

Radio waves and gamma rays are the same phenomenon at frequencies fourteen
orders of magnitude apart, and no single instrument observes both. Gravitational
waves cover an even wider range, and the same thing is true: the instrument is
dictated by the frequency, and the frequency is dictated by the source.

### What sets a binary's frequency

The physics that fixes the band is Kepler's third law together with the fact
that a binary cannot get closer than a few Schwarzschild radii before it
merges. The Schwarzschild radius is proportional to the mass, so the smallest
orbit a binary of mass $M$ can have is proportional to $M$ — and putting that
separation into Kepler's third law gives a merger frequency

$$
f_{\mathrm{merge}} \propto \frac{c^3}{G M} .
$$ {#eq-fmerge}

**The frequency at which a binary merges is inversely proportional to its
mass.** Two neutron stars merge at hundreds of hertz. Two $30\,M_\odot$ black
holes merge at a few hundred hertz. Two billion-solar-mass black holes merge at
around a **nanohertz** — one cycle every thirty years.

That single scaling is why the gravitational-wave sky is divided into bands,
and why each band is the exclusive property of a particular kind of source.

### The bands

| Band | Frequency | Instrument | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ground interferometers | $10$–$10^{3}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ | LIGO, Virgo, KAGRA | merging neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes |
| Space interferometers | $10^{-4}$–$10^{-1}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ | LISA | massive black hole binaries, white dwarf binaries, stellar-mass objects spiraling into massive ones |
| Pulsar timing | $10^{-9}$–$10^{-7}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ | NANOGrav and the other arrays | supermassive black hole binaries |
| Primordial | $\sim 10^{-16}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ | the polarization of the cosmic microwave background | gravitational waves from inflation |

One bookkeeping point before reading that table against @fig-spectrum. A binary
is symmetric under half a turn — swap the two objects and the mass distribution
is unchanged — so its quadrupole returns to where it started **twice** per
orbit, and it radiates at twice the orbital frequency,
$f_{\mathrm{GW}} = 2 f_{\mathrm{orb}}$. Detector bands are always quoted as
gravitational-wave frequencies, so that is what the horizontal axis below
carries.

```{python}
#| label: fig-spectrum
#| fig-cap: "The gravitational-wave sky, computed from @eq-strain-binary for four equal-mass binaries, all placed at 400 Mpc. Each track is an inspiral: as the pair spirals in, the frequency climbs and the strain rises with it as $f^{2/3}$, until the two objects merge at the marked point. Heavier binaries sit higher — a pair of billion-solar-mass black holes is a hundred million times louder than a pair of neutron stars — and end further to the left, because a heavier binary merges at a lower frequency. That is why each shaded band belongs to one kind of source. Note where the heaviest track ends: between the pulsar-timing and space bands, so arrays catch supermassive binaries during their long inspiral rather than at merger."
#| fig-alt: "A log-log graph of gravitational-wave strain, from ten to the minus twenty-four up to ten to the minus thirteen, against gravitational-wave frequency in hertz, from one nanohertz to ten kilohertz. Three vertical shaded bands are labeled, left to right: pulsar timing from about two to four hundred nanohertz, space interferometers from ten to the minus four to ten to the minus one hertz, and ground interferometers from ten to two thousand hertz. Four parallel straight tracks rise gently to the right with the same shallow slope, each ending in a filled dot. The lowest and rightmost, labeled one point four solar masses each, ends inside the ground band at a strain near three times ten to the minus twenty-three. Above it, a track labeled thirty solar masses each ends at the left edge of the ground band near six times ten to the minus twenty-two. Far higher and to the left, a track labeled one million solar masses each ends inside the space band near two times ten to the minus seventeen. Highest of all, a track labeled one billion solar masses each passes through the pulsar timing band and ends just to its right, near two times ten to the minus fourteen."
#| fig-height: 4.2

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.2))

G, c = 6.6732e-8, 2.99792456e10          # cgs
M_sun, pc = 1.9891e33, 3.0856e18
r = 400e6 * pc                            # a common distance for all four

def inspiral(m_each, decades=2.8):
    """Strain against GW frequency for an equal-mass binary, up to merger."""
    M = m_each * M_sun
    R_merge = 6 * G * (2 * M) / c**2      # a few Schwarzschild radii
    f_merge = np.sqrt(G * (2 * M) / R_merge**3) / (2 * np.pi)
    f_orb = np.logspace(np.log10(f_merge) - decades, np.log10(f_merge), 200)
    R = (G * (2 * M) / (4 * np.pi**2 * f_orb**2)) ** (1 / 3)
    h = 4 * np.pi**2 * G * M * R**2 * f_orb**2 / (c**4 * r)
    return 2 * f_orb, h                   # f_GW = 2 f_orb

bands = [("Pulsar\ntiming", 2e-9, 4e-7),
         ("Space\n(LISA)", 1e-4, 1e-1),
         ("Ground\n(LIGO)", 1e1, 2e3)]
for name, lo, hi in bands:
    ax.axvspan(lo, hi, color="#edece6", zorder=0)
    ax.text(np.sqrt(lo * hi), 4e-13, name, ha="center", va="top",
            fontsize=9.5, color=INK2, zorder=5)

tracks = [(1.4,   BLUE,   "-",   r"$1.4\,M_\odot$ each"),
          (30,    AQUA,   "--",  r"$30\,M_\odot$ each"),
          (1e6,   ORANGE, "-.",  r"$10^{6}\,M_\odot$ each"),
          (1e9,   INK2,   ":",   r"$10^{9}\,M_\odot$ each")]
for m, color, style, label in tracks:
    f, h = inspiral(m)
    ax.plot(f, h, style, color=color, zorder=3)
    ax.plot(f[-1], h[-1], "o", color=color, markersize=7,
            markeredgecolor=SURFACE, markeredgewidth=1.2, zorder=4)
    # Label above the START of each track: the tracks rise to the right, so
    # text placed above the left end sits clear of its own line.
    # The tracks rise to the right, so a label placed above the left end is
    # crossed by its own line further along; the backing box masks that.
    ax.annotate(label, (f[0], h[0]), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(2, 9), ha="left", va="bottom",
                fontsize=9.5, color=color, zorder=6,
                bbox=dict(facecolor=SURFACE, edgecolor="none", pad=1.5))

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1e-9, 1e4)
ax.set_ylim(1e-25, 1e-12)
ax.set_xlabel(r"gravitational-wave frequency  $f_{\mathrm{GW}}$  (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"strain  $h$  at 400 Mpc")
ax.grid(which="major", axis="both")
plt.show()
```

Ground-based detectors have arms of kilometers and are limited at low
frequencies by seismic noise — the ground itself moves more than the wave does.
**LISA** will be three spacecraft in a triangle with arms of about 2.5 million
kilometers, trailing the Earth around the Sun, where there is no ground to
shake. It is led by ESA with NASA participation and is expected to launch in
the mid-2030s. The bottom two rows of that table need no instrument built by
anyone: they use the Galaxy, and the early universe, as the apparatus.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about why the loudest sources in the Universe are not the easiest to detect"}
Run the numbers in the Numerical exploration tab again. A pair of supermassive
black holes produces a strain of about $10^{-16}$ at the Earth — ten thousand
times larger than GW150914, which is the most violent event ever recorded by a
human instrument.

LIGO cannot detect it, and never will, and the reason has nothing to do with
sensitivity.

A detector does not measure strain, exactly. It measures *changes* in strain,
and it has to see several cycles to tell a wave from a slow drift. The
supermassive pair takes **thirty years** to complete one orbit. Over the
fraction of a second that a LIGO measurement is sensitive to, that wave is not
a wave at all — it is a constant, and a constant stretch of both arms by the
same fraction is invisible to an instrument built to measure a difference.

To hear a thirty-year wave you need an experiment that runs for decades and a
baseline much longer than four kilometers. Both of those are the subject of the
next section.

**The general lesson is worth keeping.** Amplitude is not detectability. What
a detector can see is set by the match between the source's frequency and the
instrument's band, and only after that by how loud the source is.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-spectrum}

1. Using @eq-fmerge and the fact that two $30\,M_\odot$ black holes merge at
   around $300\ \mathrm{Hz}$, estimate the frequency at which two
   $3 \times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$ black holes merge. Express your answer both in
   hertz and as a period.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The mass ratio is $3\times10^{8}/30 = 10^{7}$, and the frequency scales as
   $1/M$, so

   $$
   f = \frac{300\ \mathrm{Hz}}{10^{7}} = 3 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{Hz} ,
   $$

   a period of $1/(3\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}) = 3.3\times10^{4}\
   \mathrm{s}$, or about nine hours. Note where that lands: not in the
   pulsar-timing band, but in LISA's. Supermassive binaries *merge* in LISA's
   band and spend the preceding millions of years inspiraling in the
   pulsar-timing band, which is why the two experiments see different stages of
   the same population.
   :::

2. A detector can only identify a wave if it observes several full cycles.
   Explain why this means a fifteen-year observing campaign cannot detect a
   wave with a period of fifty years, no matter how strong the wave is.

3. Rank these four systems by the gravitational-wave frequency they produce,
   highest first, and say which instrument in the table would detect each: two
   white dwarfs orbiting every five minutes; two neutron stars a moment before
   merger; two supermassive black holes 0.05 parsecs apart; two
   $30\,M_\odot$ black holes a moment before merger.

4. A student says that because gravitational-wave amplitude falls off only as

## Listening with pulsars

The nanohertz band cannot be reached by any instrument that can be built on or
near the Earth: the wave's period is decades and its wavelength is tens of
light-years. So the array is made out of the Galaxy instead.

### One pulsar is a clock; many pulsars are a detector

Start with a single millisecond pulsar. Its pulses arrive with extraordinary
regularity, so we can build a model that predicts every pulse arrival time for
years ahead, and then look at the **residuals** — the differences between when
the pulses actually arrive and when the model says they should.

A gravitational wave passing between us and the pulsar stretches and squeezes
the intervening space, changing the distance the pulses must travel and so
shifting their arrival times. The shift is of order the strain times the
light-travel time, which for $h \sim 10^{-15}$ over a few thousand light-years
comes out at tens of nanoseconds.

The trouble is that nanosecond-scale wandering in a single pulsar's arrival
times has a hundred explanations that are not gravitational waves: the pulsar's
own rotation is not perfectly steady, the interstellar medium between us and it
changes, our model of the Earth's own orbit is imperfect. One pulsar can never
be convincing.

**An array can.** Monitor dozens of millisecond pulsars scattered across the
sky for decades, and a passing gravitational-wave background affects all of
them — but not independently. The *same* wave passing the Earth imprints a
correlated wobble on every pulsar's residuals, and the strength of that
correlation depends only on the **angle between the two pulsars on the sky**.

### The Hellings–Downs curve

That correlation has a definite, calculable shape, derived by Ron Hellings and
George Downs in 1983 [@hellings1983]. It comes out of the quadrupolar character
of the waves — the same $+$ and $\times$ pattern from the first section, now
averaged over all the directions a wave might come from — and the derivation is
beyond what we will do here. What matters is the shape itself, and that you
recognize what it is for.

For two pulsars close together on the sky the correlation is strongly positive:
a wave stretching the space toward one is stretching the space toward the other
in much the same way. As the angle opens the correlation falls, crosses zero at
49°, and reaches a **negative** minimum at 82° — there one pulsar's path is
being stretched while the other's is squeezed, so their timing residuals move
in opposite directions. Past 122° it is positive again, rising toward 180°,
where two pulsars on opposite sides of the sky are partly correlated once more.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hellings-downs
#| fig-cap: "The Hellings–Downs curve: the expected correlation between two pulsars' timing residuals, as a function of the angle between them on the sky, for a background of gravitational waves. It is positive for close pairs, crosses zero at 49°, reaches a minimum of $-0.15$ at 82°, and turns positive again beyond 122°. The dashed line is what a drifting observatory clock would produce instead — every pair correlated by the same amount, whatever the angle. The two shapes are nothing alike, and that is the whole basis of the search: the detection is the *shape*, not the size of any one pulsar's wobble."
#| fig-alt: "A graph of correlation strength against the angle between two pulsars on the sky, from 0 to 180 degrees. A solid blue curve starts at 0.5 at zero degrees, falls steeply, crosses zero near 49 degrees, reaches a shallow minimum of about minus 0.15 near 82 degrees, then rises again, crossing zero near 122 degrees and reaching about 0.25 at 180 degrees. Three small open markers sit on the curve at the two zero crossings and the minimum, each labeled with its angle. A horizontal dashed orange line lies well above at a constant value of 0.3 across the whole range, labeled as the flat correlation a clock error would produce. A thin horizontal line marks zero."
#| fig-height: 3.7

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.7))

theta = np.linspace(0.05, 180, 800)
x = (1 - np.cos(np.radians(theta))) / 2
gamma = 1.5 * x * np.log(x) - x / 4 + 0.5

ax.axhline(0, color=AXIS, linewidth=0.9, zorder=1)
ax.plot(theta, gamma, "-", color=BLUE, zorder=3,
        label="gravitational-wave background")
ax.plot([0], [0.5], "o", color=BLUE, markersize=6,
        markeredgecolor=SURFACE, markeredgewidth=1.2, zorder=4)

ax.plot([0, 180], [0.3, 0.3], "--", color=ORANGE, zorder=2,
        label="a drifting clock, for comparison")

for th, note in ((49.3, "49°"), (82.5, "82°"), (121.8, "122°")):
    xx = (1 - np.cos(np.radians(th))) / 2
    gg = 1.5 * xx * np.log(xx) - xx / 4 + 0.5
    ax.plot(th, gg, "o", markerfacecolor=SURFACE, markeredgecolor=BLUE,
            markeredgewidth=1.4, markersize=6, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(note, (th, gg), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, -14),
                ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2, zorder=5)

ax.set_xlim(0, 180)
ax.set_ylim(-0.32, 0.62)
ax.set_xticks([0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180])
ax.set_xlabel("angle between the two pulsars on the sky (degrees)")
ax.set_ylabel("correlation strength")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

That curve is the fingerprint. Instrumental errors, clock errors and errors in
our model of the solar system all produce correlations too, but with completely
different shapes — a drifting observatory clock, for instance, correlates every
pair by the same amount regardless of angle, which is the dashed line in
@fig-hellings-downs. **Nothing but a background of gravitational waves produces
the Hellings–Downs shape**, which is why finding it in the data is the
detection.

### What the arrays can hear

The band a pulsar timing array is sensitive to is set by its observing
campaign, not by any hardware. The longest wave you can identify is one that
fits inside the total span of the data, and the shortest is one you sample
often enough to resolve:

$$
f_{\mathrm{min}} = \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{obs}}} ,
\qquad
f_{\mathrm{max}} \sim \frac{1}{2\,\Delta t} ,
$$ {#eq-pta-band}

where $T_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is the length of the campaign and $\Delta t$ the
interval between observations. For a fifteen-year data set observed every
couple of weeks, that is about $2\ \mathrm{nHz}$ to $400\ \mathrm{nHz}$ —
precisely the band where supermassive black hole binaries inspiral.

Note what @eq-pta-band implies: **the detector gets better simply by waiting.**
Every year of additional data lowers $f_{\mathrm{min}}$ and improves the
sensitivity across the whole band. There is no upgrade to install.

### A background, not a source

Almost every galaxy contains a supermassive black hole, and galaxies merge.
When two galaxies merge their black holes sink to the center of the remnant,
pair up, and eventually form a binary — and there have been enough galaxy
mergers over the history of the universe that the sky should contain a great
many such binaries at once.

Their signals overlap. What a pulsar timing array sees is therefore not one
source but a **background**: the summed hum of every inspiraling supermassive
binary in the universe, in the way that a crowded room produces a roar rather
than a conversation.

That hum has a predictable spectrum. Each binary's strain grows as
$f^{2/3}$ from @eq-strain-scaling, and the population's distribution in
frequency follows from how fast gravitational radiation drives each one through
the band. The result, worked through, is that the *power* in the timing
residuals should fall as $f^{-13/3}$.

**The North American Nanohertz Observatory for Gravitational Waves
(NANOGrav)** has been monitoring millisecond pulsars with the Green Bank
Telescope, Arecibo, the VLA and CHIME since 2004. In 2023 its fifteen-year data
set reported evidence for exactly this background, with the Hellings–Downs
correlation present at a significance of about three to four sigma
[@agazie2023]. The measured spectrum of the timing residuals is consistent with
the $f^{-13/3}$ expected from a population of supermassive binaries, though the
uncertainties are still wide enough to admit other explanations, including
gravitational waves from the early universe. Three to four sigma is evidence,
not proof; the arrays are still accumulating data, and by @eq-pta-band that
alone makes the result stronger every year.

If it holds up, it is a measurement of the whole population of supermassive
black hole binaries at once — a subject we will come back to when we look at
how supermassive black holes and their galaxies grow together.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-pta}

1. A pulsar timing array has been running for $T_{\mathrm{obs}} = 15$ years and
   observes each pulsar every 14 days.

   a. Find $f_{\mathrm{min}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{max}}$ from @eq-pta-band, in Hz.
   b. What are the corresponding wave periods, in years and in days?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** Converting the campaign length with the fraction arranged so the
   years cancel,

   $$
   T_{\mathrm{obs}} = 15\ \mathrm{yr}
     \times \frac{3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}}{1\ \mathrm{yr}}
     = 4.73 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{s} ,
   $$

   so $f_{\mathrm{min}} = 1/T_{\mathrm{obs}} = 2.1 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{Hz}$,
   or $2.1\ \mathrm{nHz}$. Likewise $2\,\Delta t = 28\ \mathrm{d} =
   2.42 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{s}$, giving $f_{\mathrm{max}} =
   4.1 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, or about $410\ \mathrm{nHz}$.
   **(b)** The periods are the campaign length and twice the cadence by
   construction: 15 years and 28 days.
   :::

2. Explain why a pulsar timing array becomes more sensitive every year without
   any change to the telescopes, and name the one thing about the band that
   does *not* improve with time.

3. Suppose a clock at the observatory runs slow by a slowly drifting amount.

   a. Would this produce correlated residuals between pulsars?
   b. How would the correlation depend on the angle between two pulsars on the
      sky?
   c. Why does this not masquerade as a gravitational-wave background?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** Yes — every pulse from every pulsar is timed against the same clock,
   so a clock error shifts all of them together. **(b)** Not at all: the shift
   is identical for every pulsar regardless of where it is on the sky, so the
   correlation is a flat line. **(c)** Because a flat correlation is not the
   Hellings–Downs shape. The angular dependence is precisely what
   distinguishes a gravitational-wave background from the errors that would
   otherwise mimic it, and it is the reason the search is built around the
   correlation rather than around any one pulsar's residuals.
   :::

4. A single supermassive binary $0.05\ \mathrm{pc}$ across produces a strain of
   about $10^{-16}$ at $400\ \mathrm{Mpc}$, while the background NANOGrav
   reports corresponds to a strain of roughly $10^{-15}$ summed over the whole
   sky. Explain how the second number can be larger than the first when it is
   made up of sources that are individually much fainter.

:::

## Summary

| Idea | Expression | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| What radiates | a time-varying mass **quadrupole** | mass and momentum are conserved, so there is no monopole or dipole radiation, and a spherical collapse emits nothing |
| Strain | $h = \Delta L / L$ | a pure number; the fractional stretching of space, and what a detector measures |
| Two polarizations | $h_+$ and $h_\times$, at 45° | stretch one transverse direction, squeeze the other, then reverse |
| Strain from a binary | $h \approx 4\pi^2 G M R^2 f_{\mathrm{orb}}^2 / c^4 r$ | bigger for larger masses, faster orbits and nearer sources |
| The same thing with Kepler | $h \propto M^{5/3} f_{\mathrm{orb}}^{2/3} / r$ | the chirp rate gives the mass, and the mass plus the amplitude give the distance — a standard siren |
| Distance dependence | $h \propto 1/r$, not $1/r^2$ | twice the sensitivity is twice the range and eight times the event rate |
| Detector geometry | two perpendicular arms | the wave squeezes one while stretching the other, so the *difference* is measurable when a single length is not |
| Merger frequency | $f_{\mathrm{merge}} \propto c^3 / GM$ | heavier binaries merge at lower frequencies, which is what divides the spectrum into bands |
| Pulsar timing band | $f_{\mathrm{min}} = 1/T_{\mathrm{obs}}$, $f_{\mathrm{max}} \sim 1/2\Delta t$ | about 2 to 400 nHz, and it improves just by waiting |
| The signature | the Hellings–Downs curve | correlation between pulsars as a function of their angular separation; nothing else produces that shape |

A century after they were predicted, gravitational waves have gone from an
untestable consequence of general relativity to a working branch of
observational astronomy, and the two ends of the spectrum are telling us about
two different populations of black holes. Ground-based detectors now find
stellar-mass mergers at better than one a week; pulsar timing arrays are
closing in on the collective hum of supermassive binaries across the whole sky.
Both of those populations have to come from somewhere. Next we turn to how
stars live and die, and therefore to where stellar-mass black holes come from
in the first place.
